en.title: Moonraker's Secret Sound: The Close Encounters Leitmotif Explained
en.summary: Did you catch that familiar five-note melody during a tense Bond infiltration? The iconic sound from **Close Encounters of the Third Kind** surprisingly echoed in 1979's **Moonraker**, sparking a delightful mystery for fans.
en.body:
While watching **James Bond** infiltrate Hugo Drax's Venetian lab in **Moonraker**, a keen-eared viewer might have noticed a very specific musical cue. As two scientists enter a secured room, they type a five-number passcode into a keypad, each press generating a distinct musical note. The resulting melody—a simple, five-note pattern—sounded remarkably familiar to many, echoing the unmistakable theme from Steven Spielberg's 1977 science fiction masterpiece, **Close Encounters of the Third Kind**. The question immediately arises: what is this iconic extraterrestrial motif doing in a Bond film?

The surprising answer lies in a shared cinematic zeitgeist and a strategic pivot by EON Productions. **Moonraker**, released in 1979, was originally intended to be **James Bond**'s next adventure, adapting Ian Fleming's novel of the same name. However, the colossal success of George Lucas's **Star Wars** in 1977, which tapped into a massive public fascination with space, prompted producers to re-evaluate. To capitalize on this burgeoning "space craze," EON decided to shift the focus of **Moonraker** towards a more overtly sci-fi narrative, mirroring the galactic adventures that were captivating audiences worldwide.

## The Spielberg Connection

It's also worth noting the fascinating personal connection between Steven Spielberg and the Bond franchise. Following the critical and commercial triumph of his 1975 blockbuster **Jaws**, Spielberg famously reached out to **Albert R. "Cubby" Broccoli**, the long-time producer of the James Bond films. Spielberg expressed his lifelong ambition to direct a Bond film, having been inspired by **Dr. No** since its release. While Spielberg never did direct a Bond film, his profound influence on the era's cinematic landscape, particularly with **Close Encounters of the Third Kind**, undoubtedly permeated the industry. The inclusion of the **Close Encounters** leitmotif in **Moonraker** can be seen as a subtle, perhaps even subconscious, nod to the director and the film that defined the era's fascination with the unknown and the cosmos.

## Fans Decode the Cosmic Connection

For fans of both franchises, this musical Easter egg is a delightful piece of cinematic trivia. It highlights how films released in close proximity, especially those that tap into similar cultural currents like the space race and the wonder of extraterrestrial life, can leave subtle imprints on one another. The fact that **Moonraker** was greenlit specifically because of the growing interest in space, a theme also central to **Close Encounters**, makes the musical reference feel less like a random coincidence and more like a thematic echo. It’s a testament to the power of iconic musical scores and how they can become instantly recognizable cultural touchstones, even appearing in unexpected corners of the cinematic universe. This shared sonic signature invites viewers to draw connections and appreciate the intricate web of influence that shapes the films we love.

## What's Next

While **Moonraker** embraced the cosmic themes of its time, the James Bond franchise has continued to evolve, exploring various genres and threats. Fans can look forward to the next chapter in the ongoing Bond saga, with details about the next film and its direction yet to be officially announced.

content_raw: I was watching Moonraker the other night (yes, of my own free will) and I noticed a rather funny reference. In the scene where Bond is in Venice, and he’s breaking into Hugo Drax’s palatial laboratory, he watches two scientists go into a locked room, typing a passcode into a keypad on the wall. Each number they press generates a musical note, and the code is five numbers long. Thus, the code is five notes long. And that melody, that five-note pattern, was really familiar. Take a look: “That sounds exactly like the theme to Close Encounters of the Third Kind !” I cried. “That ‘s the theme to Close Encounters of the Third Kind!” my husband said at almost the same time. “But what’s it doing in this movie ?” Indeed… what on earth is it doing in Moonraker? It couldn’t be a coincidence… Moonraker came out in 1979, while Close Encounters of the Third Kind came out in 1977. Moonraker is about space, and obviously, Close Encounters of the Third Kind is about space. Moonraker actually was green-lit because it was about space. In the end credits to 1977’s The Spy Who Loved Me, it is announced that “James Bond will return in… For Your Eyes Only. ” But due to the wild success of Star Wars, which was released that same year, EON decided to capitalize on the cinematic space craze and adapt Fleming’s novel Moonraker. So we looked it up. After the success of Jaws (1975) Steven Spielberg contacted Albert R. Broccoli (whose nickname was “Cubby”) and offered to direct a Bond film. He said , on the podcast, The Rest Is Entertainment “I’d always wanted to make a James Bond film from the day I saw Dr No.” In a 2016 interview with Michael Ball on his BBC Radio 2 show , he elaborated, “ I called Cubby Broccoli twice, and after Jaws which was such a huge success, I thought ‘Hey people are giving me final cut now.’ So I called up Cubby and offered my services but he didn’t think I was right for the part… ‘Then even after Close Encounters [of the Third Kind came out and was a big hit – once again – I tried to get on a Bond film.” He told The Rest Is Entertainment, “Cubby called me again after Close Encounters came out and that was a big hit … and said, we’d like to use the five notes in Moonraker . And I said, I’ll make you a deal. I’ll give you permission to use the five notes if you let me direct a Bond film. And he said, nope. But I gave him the five notes anyway.” He joked to Michael Ball in 2016, “…N ow they can’t afford me. So Barbara, forget it.” So there you have it… the Broccoli-Spielberg connection we’ve all been waiting for!
